title: The Three Questions That Will Move Your Career
author: Lead With Kelly
summary: Lead With Kelly argues that careers stall not from lack of ability but from avoiding three uncomfortable questions. (1) 'What am I doing that will keep me from getting promoted?' -- not 'How am I doing?' which produces polite non-answers. The author finally asked this after being passed over for a role and heard: 'People were just more comfortable with the other guy.' This broke the 'why not me' loop and gave clarity about trust rather than performance. (2) 'Do people experience me the way I think they do?' -- discovering the gap between intended conviction and perceived arrogance, between intended challenge and perceived disrespect for what was already working. Leadership is built on how others experience you, not how you see yourself; the gap doesn't shrink by justifying intent more articulately but by asking, listening, and adjusting actual behavior. (3) 'What am I optimizing for that I never actually decided to optimize for?' -- the hidden operating system: approval, stability, waiting for permission from someone senior, not wanting to look too ambitious. All three questions replace assumptions with clarity and force leaders to see their careers as the system sees them -- through perception, narrative, and an optimization function they didn't know was running.
points: * The question that changes things: 'What am I doing that will keep me from getting promoted?' demands a real answer rather than reassurance -- the discomfort of asking is the price of the clarity. * The gap between intent and experience: leadership is built on how others experience you, not on how you see yourself; the gap doesn't shrink through better explanations of intent but through asking, listening, and adjusting actual behavior. * Hidden optimization functions run underneath every career: approval-seeking, stability-seeking, waiting for external permission, not wanting to seem too ambitious -- these were installed at some point and have been silently shaping every decision since. * The pattern underlying all three questions: they replace assumptions with clarity and force leaders to see their careers as the system sees them -- through perception, narrative, and the optimization function running beneath conscious awareness. * The cost of not asking: a career that quietly bends toward the path of least resistance, year after year, until one day the leader looks up and realizes they have been stuck for longer than they thought.
quotes: The questions you avoid are the ones doing the most damage.
People were just more comfortable with the other guy.
Leadership is not built on how you see yourself. It's built on how others experience you.
That gap mattered more than I realized. Because the people around me weren't responding to my intent. They were responding to their experience of me.
Every career has a hidden optimization function, a quiet set of priorities running underneath everything you do.
The work never speaks. The system speaks, and the information you've chosen not to gather determines what it says about you.
The ones who ask better questions don't stay the same for long.
